clue.text: Chapter on area of Italy and area of England

parts.note: C is the standard abbreviation for chapter
Umbria is a region of central Italy

explanation.surface: A guidebook chapter covering one region of Italy and another of England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' here means placed before: the chapter letter sits on top of the Italian region.
explanation.definitionFit: Cumbria is a county in the far north-west of England, home of the Lake District.

clue.text: Very nearly got ace — iron club's new

indicators.note: something made new is remade, so the letters before it are formed afresh

parts.note: the letters of these words, ignoring the dash and apostrophe

explanation.surface: A golfer nearly scored a hole in one with a brand-new iron.
explanation.walkthrough: The golf picture of an ace and an iron club is pure camouflage; all fifteen letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes an attempt that came agonisingly close to success but fell just short of the prize.

clue.text: Give out cards incorrectly? Maiden ladies confused

parts.note: M is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for a maiden over

indicators.note: confused things are muddled out of order, so the word before it is rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Elderly spinsters at the card table get muddled and hand out the wrong cards.
explanation.walkthrough: Maiden ladies look like one phrase, but maiden gives a single letter and only ladies is mixed up.
explanation.definitionFit: To misdeal is to make a mistake when distributing cards to the players in a game.

clue.text: Arrive with leader of group, extremely rich

parts.note: to roll in is to arrive casually

indicators.note: the leader of anything is at its front, so only the opening letter of the next word counts

parts.note: first letter of group

explanation.surface: A wealthy newcomer turns up at the head of a band.
explanation.walkthrough: Rolling is short for 'rolling in it', informal for having plenty of money.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally someone rolling, or rolling in money, is very wealthy indeed.

clue.text: Film at cinema, too darn silly

indicators.note: silly means foolish and disordered, so the preceding letters are jumbled

parts.note: all the letters of these words

explanation.surface: A grumpy moviegoer complains that the picture at the cinema was far too silly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Film' looks like the subject of the complaint, but it is the definition, and the rest of the clue is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: An animated cartoon is a kind of motion picture made from drawings photographed in sequence.

clue.text: Infantryman in base one has gone inside to join

parts.note: the foot is the base of something, as of a hill

indicators.note: something that has gone inside sits within another word, so it is placed in the middle

parts.note: to solder is to join metal with molten alloy
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A recruit at the army base has gone inside to sign up.
explanation.walkthrough: The numeral goes inside the joining word, which then follows the base.
explanation.definitionFit: A foot soldier is an ordinary soldier who fights on foot, which is what an infantryman does.

clue.text: This may describe a murder at the outset on stage

parts.note: first means at the start
a degree is a stage or step in a process

explanation.surface: A detective story where the killing happens in the opening scene on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: The theatrical reading of 'stage' misleads; it means a step or level.
explanation.definitionFit: First-degree murder is the most serious category in US law, premeditated and deliberate killing.

clue.text: Yorkshire cricketer put down — one must be in a state

indicators.note: something that must be in another goes inside it, so the numeral is placed within the cricketer

parts.note: Wilfred Rhodes played cricket for Yorkshire and England
I is the Roman numeral one
to land is to put down, as a pilot does an aircraft

explanation.surface: A Yorkshire cricketer dropped from the side must be in a bad state.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a player dropped and gloomy; 'in a state' really points at a US state. Wilfred Rhodes was a famous Yorkshire and England all-rounder.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhode Island is the smallest of the fifty United States, in New England.

clue.text: Name the baritone mutilated in novel

indicators.note: something mutilated is mangled out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: all the letters of these words

explanation.surface: A singer is asked to identify the baritone whose part was butchered in a book.
explanation.walkthrough: The opera picture hides a comic novel; all fifteen letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Three Men in a Boat is Jerome K. Jerome's 1889 comic novel about a Thames boating holiday.

clue.text: Newsworthy subject, article on lake

indicators.note: in a down answer one thing on another sits above it, so the article comes before the lake

parts.note: a topic is a subject of discussion
a is the indefinite article
L is the abbreviation for lake on maps

explanation.surface: A newspaper editor picks a newsworthy subject: an article about a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'article' looks like a newspaper piece, but it is the grammatical article.
explanation.definitionFit: Something topical concerns current affairs, making it relevant to the news of the day.

clue.text: Nutters disrupted trial

indicators.note: disrupted means thrown into disorder, so the letters of the word before are reordered

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Some crazy people interrupted a court case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trial' suggests a courtroom, but it means a practice attempt. Nutters is British slang for mad people.
explanation.definitionFit: A test run is a rehearsal or experimental run to check that something works properly.

clue.text: Dog, mine, chased by farm animal

indicators.note: something chased by another has it coming along behind, so the animal follows the mine

parts.note: a pit is a coal mine
a bull is a male farm animal

explanation.surface: My dog is being chased round the field by a farm animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mine' reads as a possessive in the surface but is a noun meaning a pit.
explanation.definitionFit: A pit bull is a muscular terrier breed, a type of fighting dog.

clue.text: Men — they let of steam, reportedly

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the answer is what the phrase sounds like

parts.note: geysers are hot springs that release jets of steam

explanation.surface: Men are said to need to let off steam.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed 'let of' is the source's slip for 'let off'. In British speech geyser is pronounced like geezer, slang for a man.
explanation.definitionFit: Geezer is British slang for a man or bloke, often an older one.

clue.text: Daily could be thinner after start of cutbacks

indicators.note: one thing after another follows it, so the thinner word comes second
the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: first letter of cutbacks
leaner means thinner

explanation.surface: A newspaper could become thinner after spending cuts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daily' suggests a newspaper, but in Britain a daily is a cleaning lady who comes in each day.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage a daily is a domestic help who comes in to clean, so a cleaner.

clue.text: Extremely rough at a New York plant

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only the outermost letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of rough
taken as written
taken as written
NY is the standard abbreviation for New York

explanation.surface: A visitor finds a New York factory very rough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plant' reads as an industrial site in the surface but means a botanical one.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhatany is a South American shrub whose root was used medicinally as an astringent.

clue.text: One levelling charges, copper, in nasty scare

indicators.note: placing one thing in another puts it inside, so the metal symbol goes within the mixed letters
nasty suggests something ugly and twisted, so the word after it is rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

explanation.surface: A police officer levelling charges gets a nasty fright.
explanation.walkthrough: 'copper' looks like a policeman, but it is the metal whose chemical symbol is Cu.
explanation.definitionFit: An accuser is a person who brings or levels an accusation or charge against someone.

clue.text: Going round in the morning determined to catch one

parts.note: a.m. means in the morning

indicators.note: to catch something is to hold it, so the numeral is held inside the next word

parts.note: bent on something means determined to do it
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone making the rounds in the morning, determined to catch somebody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going round' sounds like an activity, but it is an adjectival sense of surrounding.
explanation.definitionFit: Ambient describes the surrounding environment, such as ambient temperature, which encircles everything.

clue.text: Royal household officer may give praise, we hear, to former PM

indicators.note: we hear signals something spoken, so the word is written as it sounds, not as spelt

parts.note: to laud is to praise
Neville Chamberlain was British Prime Minister from 1937 to 1940

explanation.surface: A senior courtier may compliment a former Prime Minister.
explanation.walkthrough: In non-rhotic British speech laud and lord sound the same; only the first part is a homophone.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lord Chamberlain is the most senior official of the British Royal Household.

clue.text: Dear dowager harassed in tube station

indicators.note: someone harassed is flustered and in disarray, so the letters before it are rearranged

parts.note: all the letters of these words

explanation.surface: A sweet elderly widow is hassled on the London Underground.
explanation.walkthrough: The tube is London's Underground railway; Edgware Road is one of its stations.
explanation.definitionFit: Edgware Road is a station on the London Underground, served by several lines.

clue.text: Macabre story about Herts town

indicators.note: something macabre is grotesque and distorted, so the word after it is rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
on means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A grisly tale set in a Hertfordshire town.
explanation.walkthrough: Herts is the abbreviation for Hertfordshire, a county north of London; Royston is a market town there.
explanation.definitionFit: Royston is a market town in north Hertfordshire, near the Cambridgeshire border.
